name: Eye color change surgery (keratopigmentation / iris implants)
lead: Eye color change surgery refers to procedures intended to alter the apparent color of healthy eyes. Two approaches are discussed: cosmetic iris implants, such as NewColorIris and BrightOcular, which are placed inside the eye in front of the natural iris, and keratopigmentation, in which pigment is deposited in the cornea [1][2][3].

Published literature on cosmetic iris implants consists largely of case reports and case series describing complications including corneal decompensation, raised eye pressure, inflammation and vision loss [1][2][4][5]. A 2023 review states that iris implants were designed for conditions such as aniridia and are not approved by regulators anywhere for cosmetic use in healthy eyes [1].
infobox: Iris implants not approved for cosmetic use anywhere, per a 2023 review [1]
BrightOcular described as removable [3]; keratopigmentation difficult to control [3]

paras: Iris implants were first described for treating photophobia and glare from aniridia, coloboma and other iris defects; the same devices have been used cosmetically in healthy eyes [1]. The earlier NewColorIris implant is reported to have a record of high ocular morbidity and is no longer in use, while a newer BrightOcular design added grooves intended to lessen iris contact and permit fluid flow [5].

Corneal tattooing, or keratopigmentation, has been used for centuries to mask corneal scars; Wikipedia traces it to Galen in the second century and notes that femtosecond-laser methods (FLAAK) are now used on healthy eyes to change color and have become popular on social media [3]. Reported complications of corneal tattooing in general include redness, keratitis, ulceration and fading or unpredictable results [3].

A 2016 case series of patients who had BrightOcular implants placed solely for cosmetic reasons reported iritis, glaucoma and corneal decompensation [5], and a 2015 JAMA Ophthalmology report linked a newer cosmetic implant to corneal endothelial cell loss and iritis [6]. Case reports describe progressive corneal edema and glaucoma needing trabeculectomy and implant removal [2], and complications emerging 15 years after an uneventful procedure [4]. The 2023 review attributes harms to mechanical irritation of angle structures, chronic inflammation, pigment dispersion and endothelial cell loss [1].
No controlled trials of cosmetic iris implants or keratopigmentation for eye color change were found. Evidence consists of case reports and case series [1][2][4][5][6].

timeline.event: JAMA Ophthalmology report of endothelial cell loss and iritis with a new cosmetic implant [6].

card.summary: Surgery to change eye color via implants or corneal pigment; published reports mainly document serious complications.
card.note: Cosmetic iris implants are not approved anywhere; vision-threatening complications reported.

quick.overview:
Two kinds of procedure aim to change eye color: silicone implants placed in front of the iris, and keratopigmentation, which tints the cornea.

The medical literature on cosmetic implants is mainly case reports of complications.
quick.mechanism: Implants cover the natural iris with a colored disc; keratopigmentation deposits pigment in corneal layers, with femtosecond lasers used in newer versions.
quick.risks: Reported problems include corneal damage, glaucoma, inflammation and vision loss. A 2023 review says cosmetic iris implants are not approved by regulators anywhere.
